sources.title: The Sopranos: 10 years since it finished, it's still the most masterful show ever

discussion.body: The suspicion was reasonable: a mobster in therapy was already the premise of a current comedy, so a TV version would have looked like the laziest possible move. The box set did the persuading.
The format may have done as much as the quality: the box set invites the single-sitting plunge that turns a skeptical viewer into a convert.

items.title: A Guardian writer resisted The Sopranos as a suspected Analyse This spin-off
items.body:
The Guardian writer initially resisted The Sopranos in 1999 because it arrived at the same time as Analyse This, the comedy starring Robert De Niro as a mafia boss who enlists a psychiatrist's help. The writer suspected a brazen attempt to make a TV spin-off from the same premise.

The box set of the first series corrected that. The writer watched it in practically a single sitting, pausing only for snacks and toilet breaks, curtains drawn. The critic called it a new mode of television, one that showed the medium could exceed cinema.

sources.title: Ancient Theories of Soul

discussion.body: The tempting move is to collapse the two senses: Snell suggested that the thing risked in battle is the same thing that endures as a shade, and the suggestion is called plausible but unverifiable.
Why demand a single metaphysics? A poem can use 'soul' for the thing risked in battle and for the shade that remains without turning the two into one defined substance.

items.title: In the Homeric poems, the soul is what you risk in battle and what becomes a shade
items.body:
The Homeric poems use 'soul' in two distinguishable, probably related, ways. It is something risked in battle and lost in death. It is also what at death departs from a person's limbs and travels to the underworld, where it has a more or less pitiful afterlife as a shade or image of the deceased.

The presence of soul distinguishes a living body from a corpse.

sources.title: NASA’s Hubble Charts Path for Roman with Gravitational Lenses

discussion.body: The elegant trick is that dark matter never has to be seen directly: the visible mass comes up short, and the shortfall is measurable.
Fair, but I'd put it more cautiously: this is an inference from a mass budget, not a direct detection of the invisible stuff.

items.title: A cosmic lens weighs a galaxy by how much it bends light
items.body:
Gravitational lensing occurs when the mass of a foreground object, such as a galaxy, warps spacetime, bending and magnifying light from whatever lies behind it. By studying the distortion of a background galaxy, researchers can determine how much mass the foreground galaxy contains.

Visible matter is not enough to account for that distortion, so the same measurement lets researchers calculate both the foreground galaxy's mass and how much dark matter it contains. Dark matter is the invisible substance that makes up the majority of mass in the universe.

sources.title: Lula says rival should be disqualified over alleged Meta interference ahead of Brazil vote

discussion.body: Each campaign has now filed a disqualification petition against the other: Lula's over alleged Meta interference, Bolsonaro's over what he says was mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.
They are not mirror images. Lula's petition accuses Meta of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro; Bolsonaro's is about mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.

items.title: Lula's campaign seeks to disqualify Flávio Bolsonaro over alleged Meta interference
items.body:
Brazil's presidential election goes to a final round on Sunday, and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro over alleged interference by Meta. In a petition filed Wednesday, the leftist incumbent accused Meta—the company behind WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook—of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.

Bolsonaro filed a counter-petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp. Meta has denied that the campaigns were treated unequally.

sources.title: Why using AI saves doctors time but won’t fix physician burnout

discussion.body: The mechanism is less a shortcut than a reallocation: the saved time is real, but it gets absorbed by other administrative work or extra appointments. That makes the scribe a productivity tool for the system, not a break for the clinician.
Maybe that is the point: if one in five use the time to add appointments, the scribe is expanding capacity. The problem may be that the system has no way to let clinicians keep the gain.

items.title: AI scribes save time; Canada's program shows where the savings go
items.body:
More than 12,000 primary care clinicians have enrolled in Canada Health Infoway's national AI scribe program, and about 5,000 Ontario physicians use AI scribes. The tools listen to a clinical visit, with the patient's consent, and automatically draft the physician's notes. The argument is that AI keeps its narrow promise of saving time, but without proper frameworks it quietly adds new burdens that absorb those savings.

In the national program, half of clinicians put the time they saved into other administrative work, and one in five used it to add appointments.

sources.title: See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape

discussion.body: Aragon's open-arms welcome stands out against the regulatory direction elsewhere: other countries have enacted rules to curb data-center expansion, and Spain's national government is weighing new restrictions. That is regulatory arbitrage as regional economic policy.

The speed has a local price: the rapid approval process for large and hyperscale facilities has left many in Aragon feeling excluded from decisions that will profoundly affect the region and their lives. Calling it arbitrage is fair; calling it a partnership is harder.

items.title: Aragon's Data Center Plans: 27 Projects, Fast Permits, and a Lot of Water
items.body:
Aragon has drawn data-center companies with promises of large tax breaks and fast-tracked planning permissions that give the facilities a special status usually reserved for the general interest of the local population.

Official documents put the buildout at 27 centers across the region, taking up about 7 square miles; some are by Spanish and other firms, but most are by American companies.

The centers are expected to consume many times the region's current electricity and to require large amounts of water to cool their servers, in one of Spain's driest regions, which has been repeatedly hit by drought.

sources.title: Healing and Memory in Ancient Greece

discussion.body: The tempting move is to make Mnemosyne the goddess of not forgetting a divine encounter, but Ahearne-Kroll's approach is more interesting: first work out what remembering such an encounter meant, then ask why memory had a place at these sanctuaries.

That can sound like a gap dressed as a method. The evidence establishes that Mnemosyne mattered at some healing sanctuaries and that she is the memory goddess; it does not give a reason, so any tidy story about why memory belonged there is speculation.

items.title: At Greek Healing Sanctuaries, the Goddess of Memory Was on the Guest List
items.body:
Before supplicants could undergo the signature incubation ritual at Asklepios's sanctuaries—spending the night in a dormitory-like building where the god would, in theory, appear in a dream and offer a miracle cure—they were asked to sacrifice to a wide range of other gods.

Mnemosyne, the goddess of memory and mother of the nine Muses, is a particularly baffling presence at some Greek healing sanctuaries: the sources say she was important there, but they do not explain why.

Ahearne-Kroll wrote in a 2014 paper that the question has to be approached indirectly, by working out what it actually meant to remember an encounter with a divinity.

sources.title: Does opting out of smart TV tracking work? Research finds “suspicious” traffic.

discussion.body: Opting out is being handled like a preference, not a boundary. That is the privacy problem in one line.
Eight operating systems across 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers is a wide sample of brands, but twelve sets is not every living room.

items.title: Samsung, Vizio and Roku TVs Continued Sending ACR Data After Opt-Outs
items.body:
A Northeastern University paper reports that smart TVs running Samsung, Vizio, and Roku operating systems continued sending data to automatic content recognition endpoints after users opted out of tracking in device settings. ACR captures video screenshots or audio clips from the TV and sends them to remote servers, where they are used for things like measuring content viewership and serving targeted ads.

The paper points to potential privacy violations from some of the biggest TV brands.

sources.title: Trump merchandise stores are closing: 'He has peaked'

discussion.body: The merch business is a mood business. The plunge from $200,000 to $20,000 a month looks less like a verdict on Trump than a sign that fans stopped feeling a performance was required.
Maybe, but the Bensalem store closed with Trump’s average approval at 44%, down from 50% when he took office. That looks more like politics than choreography.

items.title: A Trump Superstore’s $200,000 Month Became a $20,000 One
items.body:
Bill Hays shut down his Trump super store outside Knoxville, Tennessee. One day, Hays said, there was a line of 80 people out the door and sales hit $200,000 a month. By the time it closed in September, sales had fallen to just $20,000 a month.

Hays said that after the inauguration, he thought a lot of people felt their job was done and no longer had to promote MAGA or Trump. Store owners say that with the president now in his second and final term, there isn’t as much to fire up the consumer fan base and sales have softened.

sources.title: Trump ordered to answer questions under oath in BBC lawsuit

discussion.body: Trump's lawyers said in a separate filing that he could appear between 11 and 22 January next year, and disputed that he was avoiding the deposition. That is a polite way to ask a judge to move a deadline just set.
The January window may be less evasive than it looks. Depositions typically take place in a lawyer's office rather than a courtroom, with no judge physically present.

items.title: A US Judge Ordered Trump to Answer Questions Under Oath by December 11 in His BBC Suit
items.body:
Trump is suing the BBC over a Panorama episode that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the 2021 Capitol riot.

US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett said Trump must sit for the deposition by 11 December unless the discovery period is extended. Trump cancelled a previous deposition on 16 October, citing “matters of national importance” while he was campaigning in Georgia.

sources.title: ‘Tangles’ Wins Grand Jury Prize at Animation Is Film Festival

discussion.body: The Fumi Kitahara Special Jury Prize went to Iron Boy, directed by Louis Clichy. The jury praised its watercolor-like and Chinese ink-brush visuals and its roots in Clichy's memories of growing up in rural France.
Iron Boy took that special jury prize. It also won the Features Audience Award. The grand prize still went to Tangles, which makes the usual jurors-versus-crowd split look like a convenience.

items.title: A 2-D Dementia Story Framed in Stark Monochrome Wins the Grand Jury Prize at Animation Is Film Festival
items.body:
Tangles won the Grand Jury Prize at the 9th annual Animation Is Film Festival. Directed by Leah Nelson, the 2-D animated film follows a family affected by their mother's battle with dementia.

The features jury praised its fluid 2D animation and stark monochrome framing. It also said Nelson and her voice team stayed faithful to Sarah Leavitt's graphic novel, which the jury described as tackling a serious, painful subject with great beauty, honesty and a gentle touch, and it praised a flashback to 1990s-era San Francisco.

sources.title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI

discussion.body: The quietly alarming part sits upstream of the fix: the target value the policy scales on was a guess, and guesses like that fail silently until real traffic proves them wrong. Far better to take the measurement deliberately than to have the spike take it for you.

But notice how much of the recipe is really a container argument. A container you control can enforce its own admission limits and expose the exact concurrency signal the platform already publishes, instead of retrofitting a borrowed metric onto a workload it wasn't built for. So the measurement plan and the serving stack are a package deal, which is a less portable recommendation than it first looks.

items.title: Two Measured Numbers Replace a Guessed Auto Scaling Target
items.body:
AWS's walkthrough deploys Kokoro-82M in a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, then replaces a guessed auto scaling target with one derived from two measurements taken against that live endpoint. Those numbers are Q_max, the concurrency ceiling a single instance serves inside the SLO, and T_total, how long a real scale-out takes.

Synthesis is awkward to instrument: a single TTS request holds a connection open for several seconds with no token-generation loop to attach a metric to. The timing is the ugly part, since latency climbs past the SLO right when the most callers are listening.

The custom container is not incidental, either. Running Kokoro-82M in one, rather than behind a managed inference toolkit, is what makes the rest of the approach possible.

sources.title: First Nations artists pull art from University of Calgary after event inviting debate on residential schools

discussion.body: The university's statement is procedural rather than substantive: it does not endorse the views expressed by the organizers of the event, the statement said, but it is bound by regulation to permit free expression. That is a genuine bind, and also a way of not quite answering whether this particular invitation was worth issuing.

Inviting students to debate whether residential schools were genocide is not testing a live open question, since the House of Commons backed a motion in 2022 recognizing them as genocide. Arguing the other side of that at a card table is re-litigating a vote, not modelling inquiry.

What went in the art's place is the more interesting statement: in its place they left a letter to the school and sage for smudging. That is an argument too, just not one that takes questions from the floor.

items.title: Two First Nations Artists Pull Their Work From a Calgary Gallery Over a Residential-Schools Debate
items.body:
Two First Nations artists have pulled their work from the University of Calgary's gallery in protest over a controversial event on campus. The event at issue: the day before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, a group set up a table on the University of Calgary campus inviting students to debate whether residential schools were an act of genocide.

In 2022, the House of Commons backed a motion recognizing Canada's residential schools as genocide. After learning of the event on campus, the two discussed it and decided to remove their art.

sources.title: RIP BioWare: EA shuts down storied RPG studio after over three decades

discussion.body: There is something bleakly tidy about the phrasing. Thirty-odd years and an unfinished project get one clause each, as if a studio and its next game were the same size of thing.

A studio isn't its back catalogue, but the back catalogue is what people will keep arguing about. Mass Effect and Knights of the Old Republic are still the thing the name means; the argument outlives the office.
And fifty of those reported cuts land at the studio itself, which is why this reads as a BioWare story rather than a line in a spreadsheet. That's the number with a face on it.

items.title: BioWare Is Closing, and Early Work on the Next Mass Effect Ends With It
items.body:
BioWare announced on social media that it is closing after more than three decades, and that early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending. The name carries weight for what it made: Mass Effect, Dragon Age, Neverwinter Nights and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic.

Ars Technica reports that the announcement came minutes after a Bloomberg story detailing 400 job cuts across BioWare's parent company, Electronic Arts, including 50 at BioWare, based on a person familiar with the plans.

The wording is almost generous: three decades of shared adventures first, then the unfinished project in the same sentence. The reported numbers put the closure in a more ordinary frame, fifty jobs at a studio counted inside four hundred across a parent company.

sources.title: David Chase: I was annoyed that fans wanted Tony Soprano dead

discussion.body: He says what annoyed him was how many people wanted to see Tony killed, and the scale is the interesting part. One viewer wanting the character dead is a taste; a crowd wanting it starts to look like a verdict.
But the desire for closure is not the same as bloodlust. Tony is a mob boss; wanting to know whether he gets killed is the minimum curiosity the premise invites.

Maybe not bloodlust, but Chase's complaint is about the price of admission: love the character, side with him, then demand the ending that settles him. That is a strange bargain, and he is allowed to find it ungrateful.

items.title: David Chase Was Annoyed That Viewers Wanted Tony Soprano Dead
items.body:
The Guardian reports that David Chase, the creator of The Sopranos, has spoken about his irritation at viewers who wanted Tony Soprano to die at the end of the series. Chase, who directed the final episode and was the show's showrunner, said he was bothered by viewers' insistence on seeing the fate of James Gandolfini's mob boss confirmed: they wanted to know that Tony was killed.

Chase said he knew Tony was a criminal, but he asked viewers not to claim they did not love him in some way, or were not on his side in some way, after watching him for seven years.

sources.title: Venus of the Sewers

discussion.body: The mismatch is the fun: Venus, goddess of love, gets a shrine by the city's sewers. It makes the city's sacred landscape feel less like a gallery of marble ideals and more like a system that put a goddess wherever a city had a problem.
The drain may not be the point at all. What survives is a small stone circle that most visitors pass by; the idea of the shrine is doing more work than the ruin.

items.title: The Venus of the Sewers Had a Shrine in the Roman Forum
items.body: A small circle of stone in the Roman Forum is easy to pass by, but the spot was once the shrine of Venus Cloacina, the Venus of the Sewers. JSTOR Daily notes that the title seems odd for a goddess of love, but Pliny wrote about her, and surviving coins bear her name and show the shrine as it once stood: an open-air platform surmounted by two statues in flowing robes.

sources.title: ‘Obsession’ Star Inde Navarrette Says Gen Z Wants Films ‘Where We’re Not Being Sold. We Are Tired of Ads in Movies and Product Placement’

discussion.body: The interesting part is that Navarrette isn't arguing for originality as an aesthetic category so much as a transaction: not just original stories, but assurance that young moviegoers aren't being force-fed corporate slop.
But she's not a purist: she calls ads in movies fundamental and admits she grew up quoting fun commercials like State Farm and Aflac; the objection is to the pitch, not to commerce existing.

items.title: Obsession Cost Under $1 Million and Pulled In $522 Million; Its Breakout Star Says Gen Z Doesn't Want to Feel Sold
items.body:
Inde Navarrette, an Obsession breakout, went on The Kyle Buchanan Show to give Hollywood advice about keeping Gen Z interested in theaters. Her line: Gen Z just wants to go to something where it doesn't feel like it's being sold.

Obsession turned Navarrette and co-star Michael Johnston into overnight sensations with a $522 million global haul. Obsession, the Focus Features horror movie, was produced for under $1 million and is one of the most profitable in Hollywood history.

sources.title: Presocratic Philosophy

discussion.body: That selectivity cuts both ways. It can distort, but it also means the archive is an argument about what later writers found worth preserving—and occasionally new material still comes to light.

New material doesn't make the chain transparent; it still has to be read through sources whose line often runs indirectly through Hippias, Aristotle, Theophrastus and Simplicius. Fragmentary evidence complicates any clean reconstruction.

items.title: Most Presocratics Wrote a 'Book.' No Complete Work Survives.
items.body:
Most Presocratics wrote at least one 'book'—short prose pieces, sometimes poems—but no complete work survives. The line back to them is often indirect, depending on the work of Hippias, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Simplicius and other ancient philosophers who had direct access.

All sources for the fragments and testimonia made selective use of the material, according to their own varied interests in the early thinkers.

sources.title: The ancient world teemed with birds; now we think with them

discussion.body: Owls and swallows on public buildings is the part I keep turning over. We talk about urban nature as if it were a new amenity we are finally installing, when the classical city was already full of it.

Careful with the idyll, though. The same inventory has kites and ravens scavenging the streets. That is a city processing its own refuse, which is a fine thing for a raven and a slightly less romantic picture of antiquity.

items.title: Nightingales Sang in the Suburbs of Athens and Rome
items.body:
History can do what a photograph from space does: give you a jolt of distance. The Mediterranean world of 2,500 years ago would have looked and sounded conspicuously different from the one we picture. Nightingales sang in the suburbs of Athens and Rome. Wrynecks, hoopoes, cuckoos and orioles lived within the city limits, along with a teeming host of warblers, buntings and finches; kites and ravens scavenged the streets; owls, swifts and swallows nested on public buildings.

Out in the countryside, eagles and vultures soared overhead, and people could watch cranes, storks and wildfowl move through on migration. The detail that sticks is the nesting: civic architecture doubling as habitat, owls on public buildings. It is a useful corrective to the assumption that wildlife is what you travel out of town to find.

sources.title: Healing walk in memory of teen hit by truck on Ont. highway highlights need for more pedestrian safety efforts

discussion.body: The phrase “for the long term” is the telling part. The crossing and path are the durable answer, while the shuttle is the item already under study.
I’d bet on the shuttle arriving first anyway. Planning studies are underway for it; the crossing and path are framed as long-term work, which sounds like the slower track.

items.title: A Healing Walk on Highway 11, and the Long-Term Push for a Pedestrian Crossing
items.body:
Noreen Agnew is leading a healing walk along Highway 11 to raise awareness about pedestrian safety, saying she does not want her 17-year-old daughter’s death to be in vain. Markenna Agnew died on Nov. 28, 2025, after being struck by a transport truck while walking from Long Lake #58 First Nation to Longlac in northwestern Ontario.

For the longer term, Long Lake #58 First Nation is leading efforts to build a pedestrian crossing and walking path between the community and Longlac. Planning studies are also underway for a community safety shuttle program, with support from Indigenous Services Canada.

The crossing and path are framed as long-term work; the shuttle program is still in planning. A healing walk can make a stretch of highway visible, while a crossing, a path or a shuttle is the kind of thing that would change the trip between the two communities.
